mexico_quotation.non_substantial: One 41-word sentence from the first volume provides the selected explanation of laughter for direct comparison to the German. It leaves the examples and rest of the treatise out, and cannot replace reading the book.
mexico_quotation.normal_exploitation: The attributed sentence is displayed with the German original and philosophical context for research and comparison. It does not substitute for the treatise or its translation; the assessment is confined to this precise display.
mexico_quotation.source_integrity: The text and punctuation are compared to the printed p. 76 image, with only line breaks and line-end hyphenation joined. The author, both translators, edition, source and printed page are named; Kemp’s death date is not asserted.

§13 p70.text: The cause of laughter in every case is simply the sudden perception of the incongruity between a concept and the real objects which have been thought through it in some relation, and laughter itself is just the expression of this incongruity.
§13 p70.alignment: The English sentence corresponds to the complete German sentence: laughter arises solely from suddenly perceived incongruity between a concept and real objects thought under it, and is itself the expression of that incongruity.

Personally read German 1859 p. 70 and English p. 76: the complete sentence and punctuation match the print, without omitted emphasis, and preserve the universality, exclusivity, sudden perception, concept and real objects, and laughter as expression of the incongruity. The undated seventh-edition title page names R. B. Haldane and J. Kemp; the catalogue year is distinguished from the title-page evidence.

mexico_quotation.assessment: A single 41-word sentence from the long published first volume is presented with the German original and a specific interpretive thesis about laughter and incongruity. The focused quotation supports that comparison without reproducing the surrounding examples and is no substitute for the treatise. LFDA 148(I) requires source attribution, unchanged quotation and no effect on normal exploitation. This judgment concerns this exact display and must be revisited if aggregate excerpts or the presentation change; it does not resolve other jurisdictions or infer an unknown death date.
